papers.note: The most cited general LLM survey, covers pre-training, post-training, utilisation and evaluation in one frame.
papers.title: A Survey of Large Language Models
papers.abstract: The rapid evolution of large language models (LLMs) has driven a transformative shift in artificial intelligence (AI), reshaping both research paradigms and practical applications. Distinguished from their predecessors by unprecedented scale and advanced capabilities, LLMs necessitate new frameworks for understanding their development, behavior, and societal impact. This survey systematically reviews recent advancements in LLM techniques across four key dimensions: (1) pre-training methodologies, which establish core model capabilities through large-scale self-supervised training, architectural innovations, and data curation strategies; (2) post-training techniques, including supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning, which adapt foundational models to downstream tasks and enhance their alignment and safety; (3) utilization strategies, such as in-context learning, prompt engineering, and agentic reasoning, that optimize real-world deployment and enable effective interaction with external environments; and (4) evaluation methods, encompassing benchmarks for key ability dimensions such as core language capabilities, reasoning, and safety, which support comprehensive and reliable assessment of model performance. Additionally, we identify critical research issues, including those concerning theoretical foundations, efficient scaling, alignment, and agentic capability, and highlight the open challenges they present.
papers.explain_beginner: A large language model is what powers products like ChatGPT. This paper is the most comprehensive tour of how one gets built from scratch, from the huge dataset it learns on, to the fine-tuning that teaches it to follow instructions, to the tests used to prove it works. If you want a single reading list to understand modern AI, this is the map.
papers.explain_business: When executives ask "how do these things actually work end to end", this is the answer. It shows that building a competitive LLM requires four distinct capabilities — massive training data + compute, alignment and safety tuning, an application layer that turns raw models into products, and evaluation infrastructure — and that most vendors specialise in one or two of them. That framing is useful for build-versus-buy decisions and for understanding where an AI supplier's real moat sits.
papers.explain_practitioner: Zhao et al. give a four-part taxonomy of the LLM lifecycle — pre-training, post-training (SFT + RLHF), utilization (in-context learning, prompt engineering, agents) and evaluation — and cover the leading techniques in each. It is the field's de facto survey, kept current across arXiv versions, and its 4,600+ citations reflect that it is where most graduate courses and industry onboarding docs start. Use it as a citation-mining tool rather than a linear read.

papers.note: The most cited general survey of the field, covering the GPT, LLaMA and PaLM families, training datasets, and evaluation metrics. A reasonable first read for anyone needing the shape of the field rather than a single result.
papers.title: Large Language Models: A Survey

papers.note: Tested leading models against 2,400 real intensive-care cases and found they diagnosed worse than physicians and did not follow treatment guidelines, which is the sharpest published rebuttal to the argument that passing medical exams implies clinical readiness.
papers.title: Evaluation and mitigation of the limitations of large language models in clinical decision-making
papers.explain_beginner: Researchers tested leading AI language models on 2,400 real intensive care cases to see if they could diagnose patients like doctors do. Despite performing well on medical exams, these AI systems diagnosed incorrectly far more often than physicians, ignored established medical guidelines, and struggled to understand lab results. The findings show that passing written exams doesn't mean AI is ready for actual patient care, highlighting important gaps between test performance and real-world medical practice.
papers.explain_business: This research demonstrates that deploying current AI language models in clinical settings would harm patient outcomes. Despite strong performance on licensing exams, these systems diagnose incorrectly, ignore medical guidelines, and struggle with practical clinical tasks. Organizations considering AI-assisted medical decision support must recognize that test scores do not validate clinical readiness. Investment in AI healthcare solutions requires validation against realistic patient data and clinical workflows before implementation.
papers.explain_practitioner: We evaluated state-of-the-art LLMs against a curated dataset of 2,400 intensive care cases covering four abdominal pathologies using a realistic clinical simulation framework. Results demonstrated significantly lower diagnostic accuracy than physicians across all conditions, failure to adhere to diagnostic and treatment protocols, and inability to process laboratory values. Models proved sensitive to information ordering and instruction following. The study provides both a benchmark dataset and evidence that current LLMs require substantial improvements before clinical deployment.

papers.note: Separates formal linguistic competence, knowing the rules, from functional competence, using language in the world, and argues models are strong on the first and patchy on the second. The distinction is now standard vocabulary in the debate.
papers.title: Dissociating language and thought in large language models

papers.note: Peer reviewed survey linking architecture choices to downstream limitations across biomedicine, vision language and code.
papers.title: Large language models (LLMs): survey, technical frameworks, and future challenges
papers.explain_beginner: This paper surveys large language models, which are advanced AI systems that understand and generate human language. The research reviews how these models work, examines their use across different fields like medicine, image understanding, and software coding, and explores what they do well and where they fall short. The findings help readers understand current AI capabilities and suggest areas needing improvement for future progress.
papers.explain_business: This survey identifies where large language models currently succeed and fail across practical applications including medical analysis, visual understanding, and software development. It reveals that while these systems show promise, fundamental limitations exist requiring new approaches. Organizations should understand these capability boundaries when planning AI deployment and recognize that continued investment in novel methodologies is necessary for meaningful advances beyond current model performance.
papers.explain_practitioner: This comprehensive survey examines large language model architectures and their implementation across multiple domains. The authors analyze foundational concepts including embeddings and deep learning techniques, review major model variants such as GPT-4 and PaLM, and document their applications in text generation, multimodal tasks, biomedicine, and code synthesis. The work systematically catalogs architectural design choices, identifies performance limitations across different tasks, and proposes new research directions for overcoming current constraints.

papers.note: Early multidisciplinary record of the capability and societal impact questions that later became regulatory text.
papers.title: Understanding the Capabilities, Limitations, and Societal Impact of Large Language Models
papers.explain_beginner: Researchers from multiple fields gathered to discuss GPT-3, a powerful artificial intelligence system that can generate human-like text. They explored two main questions: what this technology can and cannot do, and how it might affect society if many people use it. By bringing together experts in computer science, linguistics, philosophy, and policy, they created a comprehensive overview of both the technical strengths and weaknesses of these systems, as well as their broader social implications.
papers.explain_business: This early analysis documented critical questions about large language models' practical capabilities and real-world risks before widespread deployment. For decision-makers considering adoption or regulation, the findings provide a multidisciplinary assessment of what these systems can reliably do versus their failure modes, alongside their potential societal effects. This foundational work informed subsequent policy discussions and remains relevant for understanding which use cases are appropriate and what safeguards matter most.
papers.explain_practitioner: A multidisciplinary workshop convened in October 2020 to examine GPT-3's technical capabilities, limitations, and societal impact. Participants included researchers from OpenAI, Stanford HAI, and other institutions with expertise spanning computer science, linguistics, philosophy, political science, and policy. The group conducted structured discussion addressing two core research questions: the technical performance boundaries of large language models and their societal consequences at scale. Results were synthesized into a detailed summary organized around these two primary themes.

papers.note: Focuses on scaling trade-offs and on where chain-of-thought behaviour comes from in pre-training data, rather than treating emergence as unexplained.
papers.title: A Survey on Large Language Models with some Insights on their Capabilities and Limitations
papers.explain_beginner: This paper surveys large language models, the AI systems behind tools like ChatGPT. Researchers examined how these models work, why they perform so well at language tasks, and discovered interesting abilities they develop beyond their original training, such as reasoning and coding. The paper explains how feeding more data and computing power improves performance, explores real-world uses in medicine and law, and investigates where thinking abilities come from in their training data rather than treating these skills as mysterious.
papers.explain_business: This research demonstrates that LLMs provide substantial value across healthcare, finance, education, and legal sectors with domain-specific applications. However, organizations must understand that capability improvements require careful investment in data and computing resources, with associated trade-offs to evaluate. The paper emphasizes that reasoning abilities depend on training data composition, suggesting data quality matters for deployment. By connecting performance to measurable factors rather than treating improvements as unpredictable, the survey helps executives make informed decisions about LLM adoption, investment levels, and risk management in increasingly complex operational environments.
papers.explain_practitioner: This survey examines transformer-based LLMs, analyzing scaling laws showing how data and computational investment drive performance improvements across language tasks. The authors investigated emergent capabilities including commonsense reasoning and code generation, with particular focus on Chain-of-Thought and Plan-of-Thought mechanisms. They traced these reasoning behaviors to pre-training data patterns rather than treating emergence as unexplained. The work evaluates LLM-modulo frameworks integrating external systems for complex tasks and assesses architectural strategies, scaling trade-offs, and generalization mechanisms across diverse applications.

papers.note: Argues resemblance between model output and human language is functional rather than mechanistic, and that models are tools for studying language, not theories of it.
papers.title: The Limitations of Large Language Models for Understanding Human Language and Cognition
papers.explain_beginner: Large language models like ChatGPT can produce text that sounds remarkably human, but this paper shows the resemblance is misleading. While humans learn language through rich, interactive experiences using sight, sound, and touch alongside words, AI models learn only from massive amounts of written text. The paper argues that even though models produce similar-looking output, they work completely differently inside. Understanding how language actually develops in children and evolved in humans requires studying real human cognition, not just building better AI.
papers.explain_business: Organizations deploying large language models should recognize these systems excel at specific text generation tasks but have fundamental limitations for understanding meaning and diverse communication contexts. The practical implication is that LLMs work best as specialized tools for defined problems rather than general solutions for language understanding. Investments should prioritize clear research questions and specific use cases rather than expecting models to replicate human language capabilities broadly. Decision-makers should remain skeptical of claims that improving model performance reveals insights about human cognition.
papers.explain_practitioner: The authors apply ethological frameworks to compare LLM capabilities with human language acquisition and evolution. They distinguish between functional similarity, which models demonstrate, and mechanistic similarity, which they lack. Humans employ multimodal interactive learning; LLMs rely on unimodal text exposure at vastly larger scale. While models successfully imitate specific written forms, their architecture constrains semantic understanding and naturalistic communication. The paper concludes LLMs serve as empirical tools for targeted linguistic research rather than mechanistic theories, requiring explicit hypotheses to guide meaningful applications.

papers.note: Maps which underlying capabilities matter in which domain, and proposes evaluation tailored to the domain rather than to a general benchmark.
papers.title: Fundamental Capabilities and Applications of Large Language Models: A Survey
papers.explain_beginner: Large language models work well in many fields, but we don't fully understand which of their core strengths matter most for different jobs. This survey maps out the fundamental abilities these models possess and shows how different domains rely on different combinations of these abilities. Rather than using one-size-fits-all tests, the researchers suggest evaluating models based on the specific skills each field actually needs, making it easier to choose the right model for the job.
papers.explain_business: When deploying language models in production, selecting the right model requires understanding which capabilities matter for your specific application. This research provides a practical framework to identify which model strengths align with your domain's actual needs, whether healthcare, legal services, or financial analysis. Rather than relying on generic performance scores, companies can now evaluate models against the precise capabilities their business processes require, reducing deployment risk and improving real-world outcomes.
papers.explain_practitioner: This survey systematically documents LLM fundamental capabilities, their formation mechanisms, and interconnections, then analyzes their application across nine domains including medicine, law, finance, and software engineering. The authors establish explicit mappings between specific capabilities and domain-specific requirements, revealing that standard benchmarks often misalign with real-world performance needs. The key contribution is domain-tailored evaluation frameworks that prioritize assessing capabilities relevant to each application's unique demands rather than universal performance metrics.

papers.note: Side by side comparison of ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini on metrics, capabilities and limits, useful when a buyer asks which model to pick.
papers.title: CAPABILITIES AND LIMITATIONS OF LARGE LANGUAGE MODELS

reading.body:
Large language models perform well on formal linguistic tasks but fail predictably on functional reasoning and real-world deployment, a gap that test scores do not reveal.

The field has converged on a four-part lifecycle: pre-training at scale establishes raw capabilities, post-training through supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning adapts models to specific tasks, utilization strategies like prompt engineering extract value from deployed systems, and evaluation benchmarks measure performance. This architecture matters because it shows that capabilities are not monolithic. Models can excel at pattern matching in language—distinguishing grammatical from ungrammatical—while struggling with causal reasoning, clinical diagnosis, or adherence to domain guidelines. The distinction between formal linguistic competence and functional real-world competence is now standard vocabulary in research, and evidence from clinical testing demonstrates the gap is substantial: systems that pass medical exams diagnose worse than physicians on actual patient cases and ignore treatment protocols.

The practical implication is that scaling compute alone does not solve capability gaps that originate in architecture or training data. A model trained on internet text learns statistical patterns that resemble human language without learning the reasoning structures that underpin safe or correct deployment in high-stakes domains. Evaluation frameworks tailored to specific domains, not general benchmarks, reveal these limits more reliably. Current research does not yet explain why chain-of-thought behavior emerges from pre-training data rather than treating it as unexplained, nor does it establish whether these gaps can be closed through post-training or require architectural change.

This collection does not address the compute or energy cost of achieving these capabilities, or whether the buildings and power infrastructure required to scale pre-training will also scale the failures documented here. The papers map what models can do and cannot do at current scale. Whether continued scaling resolves the gaps remains open.
